summary: A case study of a several-hour ARPANET disruption in October 1980, when a high-priority software process ran out of control. It explains the symptoms and causes, and what lessons network designers can draw.

eli5.summary: One day a whole network jammed because one tiny part kept doing the wrong thing at top speed. This memo explains what happened and what to learn.

subtitle: A case study of how a hardware failure caused a network-wide outage.

tldr.problem: On October 27, 1980, the entire ARPANET became unusable for several hours, with no clear initial cause.
tldr.mechanism: A hardware malfunction in one IMP corrupted routing update sequence numbers, creating a cycle of three conflicting updates that IMPs kept processing instead of forwarding user traffic, starving the routing process of CPU and buffer resources.
tldr.outcome: The network was restored by patching all IMPs to ignore the faulty source, but the incident revealed vulnerabilities in the routing protocol and the need for better resource-monitoring alarms in IMP software.

today: RFC 789 documents a single incident from 1980 but shaped thinking about distributed system reliability for decades. The core lesson—that protocol design must anticipate hardware failures and provide automatic recovery—remains relevant to modern network engineering.

sections.title: The Outage
sections.content:
For several hours on October 27, 1980, the ARPANET was essentially unusable. No IMP could reliably communicate with any other IMP, and existing connections were broken. Phone calls flooded the Network Control Center from across the country, indicating the problem was not isolated but network-wide. Restarting individual IMPs did not help; once reconnected, they exhibited the same symptoms.

The incident was unusual: network-wide outages were extremely rare at the time. The need to understand what went wrong motivated this detailed case study.
sections.eli5: Imagine everyone's phones suddenly stopped working at once. Nobody knew why, and even restarting a phone didn't help—it broke again when you plugged it back in.

sections.title: The Cycle of Bad Updates
sections.content:
Investigation of IMP core dumps revealed that nearly all buffers held routing updates from a single IMP (IMP 50), all waiting to be processed. Moreover, these updates had only three distinct sequence numbers: 8, 40, and 44, and they appeared in the queue in a repeating pattern: 8, 40, 44, 8, 40, 44, ...

By the routing protocol's definition, 44 is considered LATER than 40, 40 is LATER than 8, and 8 is LATER than 44—forming a cycle. Each IMP in the network treated the three updates as a constantly newer version and re-broadcast them, creating an endless loop that consumed CPU time and buffer space that should have been used for user traffic.

The three sequence numbers had to have been corrupted by a hardware malfunction: their binary patterns showed bits dropped from a single original update 44. When retransmitted with corrupted sequence numbers, the same update appeared three times in the network simultaneously, a condition the protocol was supposed to prevent.
sections.eli5: It's like three contradictory instructions kept chasing each other in circles: 'Do A', then 'Do B', then 'Do C', then 'Do A' again. The network spent all its energy deciding which instruction was the newest instead of delivering mail.

sections.title: Recovery and Lessons
sections.content:
The engineers quickly identified IMP 50 as the source (it was down anyway during the outage) and patched all IMPs to disregard any updates from it. This restored network operation. Because the network was nearly unusable, the patch took 3 to 4 hours to distribute via the network itself rather than the usual minutes.

The underlying lesson was not simply to add more checksumming (expensive in CPU and memory). Instead, the RFC advocates for better resource monitoring alarms in the IMP software. If a process is using an excessive share of CPU or buffers, the IMP should detect it and go into a recoverable 'loader/dumper' state instead of degrading the whole network.
sections.eli5: They stopped listening to the broken telephone. But the real lesson was: machines should notice when one part is hogging all the power and shut it down before it breaks everything else.
